Prevalent

PREV-uh-lunt — stress the PREV; a prevalent trend has already prevailed almost everywhere. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Prevalent is existing very commonly or widely.

Food allergies have become far more prevalent among children over the past two decades.

Worked Example

A researcher surveys hundreds of households and finds that nearly every single one owns at least one streaming subscription. Just ten years earlier, almost none of them did.

Something found in nearly every household has become prevalent. Unlike 'popular,' which suggests people actively like something, prevalent simply describes how common or widespread it is, whether people love it or not.

Your Turn

Answer correctly to continue.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

widespread: Widespread tells you about reach: something widespread is found across a large area or population, from one coast to the other. Prevalent stresses how often it turns up within that reach — a prevalent condition appears again and again wherever you look, not just here and there across a map.

common: Common just means not rare — you meet it often, like a common cold or a common surname. Prevalent is the stronger, more clinical word: it says something has become dominant across a whole population or area, the kind of commonness researchers measure and track.

rampant: Rampant means spreading uncontrollably, and it is nearly always said of something unwanted — rampant rumors, rampant weeds. Prevalent is neutral and settled: it reports that something is now very common, without saying that it is still growing or that anyone minds.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

rare: not occurring often; uncommon

scarce: in short supply; hard to find

Where it sits · how widely it is found — noticeable → prevalent → universal

noticeable vs. prevalent: Noticeable is weaker than prevalent — something noticeable simply stands out, while something prevalent is actually found almost everywhere you look.

universal vs. prevalent: Universal is stronger than prevalent: prevalent means widespread and common, but universal means found absolutely everywhere, without a single exception.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — pre-

prefix — pre-: before (Latin)

root — -val-

root — -val-: to be strong, powerful (Latin)

suffix — -ent

suffix — -ent: state of (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Latin praevalere meant 'to be more powerful, to prevail over others.' Something prevalent has 'won out' over alternatives and become the most common.

Use the root in a new word: prevail

Use the root in a new word: prevail: After a long debate, calmer voices finally prevailed and the meeting ended peacefully.
